chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Al-Husayn ibn Saeed, from his brother Al-Hasan, from Zurara ibn Muhammad, from Sama'ah, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about a man who bought a pasture to graze in for fifty dirhams, or less or more, so he intended to include with him anyone who would graze in it and take the price from him. He (peace be upon him) said: 'Let him include with him whoever he wishes for part of what he gave, and even if he includes with him forty-nine [sheep], and his own sheep is one dirham, there is no problem.'
And if he grazed in it before he lets them in, for a month or two months or more than that, after making it clear to them, there is no problem.

And it is not for him to sell it for fifty dirhams and graze with them, nor for more than fifty and not graze with them, unless he has done work in the pasture, such as digging a well or cutting a canal, or he exerted himself in it with the consent of the owners of the pasture. So there is no problem with him selling it for more than what he bought it for, because he has done work in it, and because of that it is valid for him.
ai.seo_question: What are the conditions for sub-leasing a pasture or land in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* elucidates the permissibility of sub-leasing (*Ijarah*) and profit-sharing in agricultural contexts, emphasizing that the owner may include others in the grazing rights for a proportional share of the cost. It further clarifies that selling the pasture at a higher price is valid if the owner has invested labor or capital, such as digging a well, with the consent of the stakeholders, thereby establishing a principle of fair value addition in Shia commercial jurisprudence. The text highlights the flexibility in contractual terms, allowing for varied financial arrangements as long as the core lease agreement is respected and improvements are acknowledged.
